description: Somos un equipo de tres desarrolladores de Honduras interesados en participar en el NASA Space Apps Challenge. Nuestra idea preliminar es Rocket Mission Control, un juego educativo sobre una misión lunar en el que los jugadores administran recursos y toman decisiones. Nos interesa explorar el uso de datos y APIs de NASA para crear una experiencia interactiva. El alcance final se definirá durante el hackathon.
summary: Odyssey: Lunar Mission Designer is a browser game about designing a real lunar mission under engineering constraints. In our story, AI demand has exhausted Earth's resources, so your crew must prove that water ice at the Moon's south pole can be found and sampled. Before launch you act as mission designer: choose an objective, a launch vehicle, a lunar orbit, a CubeSat-class structure (6U/12U) and four subsystems (power, communications, instrument, propulsion) while balancing a fixed budget, mass, volume, energy and delta-v. Invalid designs cannot launch, and the game explains exactly why - overweight, over budget, too big for the rideshare, not enough delta-v for the chosen orbit, or a power deficit. Your design then becomes the mission itself: the cockpit shows the fuel, battery, mass, delta-v margin, remaining budget, Earth-Moon distance and signal delay computed from your choices and from real NASA data (JPL Horizons). On the surface only real things appear: actual landing sites and resource deposits, each labeled with its source. This addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by making resource trade-offs the core mechanic and tying every engineering decision to a visible consequence.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Odyssey puts the player in charge of a lunar mission to the south pole, targeting Shackleton crater, where permanently shadowed regions hold water ice (LCROSS measured 5.6 ± 2.9 % by mass in Cabeus). The loop is: choose a mission objective, design the spacecraft in the hangar, launch, fly, land, and explore the surface. The game locks destinations until the lunar mission is done (Mars unlocks after the Moon), keeping the focus on one complete end-to-end mission.

HOW IT WORKS

- Design phase (the heart of the game): a catalog defines 2 structures (6U, 12U), 2 launch vehicles, 2 polar orbits, 3 science objectives and 4 subsystems with 3 options each, all within a $3,500,000 budget. Size and mass references come from NASA's CubeSat 101. The rules engine (game/js/design/mission-design.js) totals mass, volume, cost, power draw versus generation and delta-v versus the orbit requirement, and blocks the launch until every constraint is met, listing each problem in plain language. There is no single right answer: a low polar orbit gives more science value but demands more delta-v and shortens Earth contact windows; a small dedicated launcher versus a rideshare secondary slot changes what fits and what you can afford.

- Flight phase: the validated design is exported to the mission. Starting fuel comes from your delta-v margin, the battery simulates your power generation versus consumption, and the cockpit screens display energy, fuel, mass, delta-v, remaining budget, Earth-Moon distance and one-way signal delay (about 1.35 s) computed from JPL Horizons data. The player must also solve the orbital computer by entering real Hohmann-transfer values (semi-major axis, departure/arrival burns, transit time, propellant) before the trip is authorized.

- Landing and surface: a VTOL landing sequence, then exploration of the lunar south pole. Only real features are shown: Apollo/Surveyor landing sites, the Marius Hills lava-tube pit, and water-ice and ilmenite deposits placed from our data files - approaching one shows its name and its source. A simplified VIPER rover (NASA's cancelled south-pole prospecting rover) is on-site with its fact sheet. Crew systems (water and rations) and checkpoints run on top of the Odyssey engine (Three.js, plain ES modules, no bundler).

WHAT BENEFITS IT HAS

It teaches mission design the way it is actually done: everything is a trade-off between budget, mass, power and delta-v, and every number the player manipulates is backed by a citable source. Being browser-based with offline fallback data files, it runs on school computers and phones with no install, no login and no API keys.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

We want players to feel that "the cheap option" is an engineering decision, not a cheat. Next, we plan to extend design consequences deeper into the surface phase - driveable rover/drone sampling of the real deposits and a generated mission report that grades the design itself - and to add co-op multiplayer in a separate branch.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, SOFTWARE

JavaScript (ES modules, no bundler), Three.js r128, Node.js (zero-dependency API server, static game server), Vite (archived design prototype), Docker Compose, GitHub Pages + Actions for publishing, HTML/CSS for the 7-slide demo, and local AI assistance (see SI section). Testing: ~70 Node check scripts (game/tests/run.cjs). Data validation against a JSON schema (api: npm run check-planets).
